blueprint.title: Recover Packed Sensor Columns
blueprint.scenario: A research scientist is reproducing a paper's latency and anomaly figures from an instrument fleet whose collector writes a compact columnar log format. The container contains the collector's SQL reporting database, format notes, damaged sample archives, and a partially implemented DuckDB SQL analysis pipeline; the original collector is not available.
blueprint.instruction_draft:
Repair and complete the SQL pipeline so it can recover measurements from the supplied packed sensor-log archives and reproduce the reference report. The pipeline must accept reordered files, duplicate pages, truncated pages, bad checksums, schema-version changes, signed value deltas, and counter resets without inventing samples; it must preserve the relationship between recovered samples, page validity, and the emitted metrics.

Create the documented entry point used by the harness and make it work on both the supplied archive and fresh hidden archives. For every hidden archive, recover at least 99.7% of the valid measurements with no invalid measurements, produce the exact deterministic per-device/day rollups and reset-aware rates, and keep the p99 latency in the report within 0.25% of the reference. The complete run must finish in under 12 seconds on the provided one-CPU container.
requirements: Provide the documented DuckDB SQL entry point and any SQL files it includes.
Read the packed sensor-log files through the supplied staging interface rather than relying on the visible sample's row order.
Decode all documented format versions, including signed zigzag deltas, dictionary-coded device identifiers, run-length encoded quality flags, and page-local time bases.
Reject truncated pages, checksum failures, impossible lengths, and malformed records without emitting measurements from them.
Handle reordered pages, duplicate pages, and duplicate records deterministically.
Recover valid measurements that occur after an invalid page or a page with a schema-version change.
Produce a validity/recovery relation whose page decisions agree with the measurements used by the reporting relations.
Compute reset-aware counter rates, excluding the interval crossing a counter reset rather than treating it as a huge positive rate.
Emit deterministic per-device/day count, mean, p99 latency, anomaly count, and recovery statistics in the documented report schema.
Achieve at least 99.7% valid-measurement recovery with zero invalid-measurement output on hidden archives.
Match the hidden reference p99 latency within 0.25%.
Complete within 12 seconds on the verifier's one-CPU workload.
environment: The Dockerfile uses FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm, installs pinned duckdb and pytest packages, and contains no network-dependent setup.
The workspace contains roughly 1,300 lines across SQL, Python archive generators, report helpers, fixtures, and operational log parsers.

A deterministic generator creates a custom SCLP (Sensor Column Log Pages) format with a fixed header, page sequence number, schema version, CRC32, column dictionaries, bit-packed quality flags, zigzag-encoded signed deltas, and a page trailer.
The generator also creates a DuckDB staging database exposing each archive page as filename, byte offset, raw hex payload, ingest batch, and observed file order.
Format documentation, schema declarations, and a small clean archive are supplied, but the clean archive does not exercise every encoding or recovery case.

The starter pipeline has relations for page staging, decoded samples, validity decisions, counter rates, and daily reports, with several deliberately incomplete or semantically inconsistent pieces; unrelated SQL handles deployment logging, configuration, and report formatting.
A compiled helper extension provides only deterministic byte access, CRC32, and population-count primitives; it is shipped without source and is not the missing solution component.

The verifier generates fresh archives with a hidden seed, varying page sizes, device counts, dictionary order, duplicate placement, corruption positions, reset frequency, and proportions of old and new schema pages.
The reference outputs are generated by the same format generator and an independent decoder, and the reference shell script investigates the supplied logs and samples before applying the SQL repair.
blueprint.internal_hint: The intended resolution is to inspect the staging schema, format notes, query plans, and recovery logs, then replace the incomplete recursive SQL decoder with a page-bounded decoder that tracks byte position and remaining length explicitly. The important fixes are mathematical rather than textual: signed zigzag values must be sign-extended before applying deltas, bit-packed flags must be consumed least-significant-bit first within each byte, and dictionary identifiers are page-local rather than archive-global. Page identity must be deduplicated by archive identity plus sequence and CRC after validation, while physical order must not affect reconstruction. Validity must be materialized once and joined by the same page key everywhere; otherwise the report can disagree with the recovered-sample count. Rate calculation must use ordered device timestamps and suppress exactly the interval whose cumulative counter decreases. A skilled engineer finds these facts by comparing decoded byte positions and counts against the generator's debug metrics, then uses EXPLAIN and a large generated archive to eliminate repeated JSON/blob expansion. The difficulty is substantial construction plus hidden data-dependent cases: the visible archive passes a naïve decoder because its dictionary order, bit alignment, and page order are unusually friendly.
blueprint.trap: A shallow solution can decode the clean sample and report plausible metrics while treating dictionary IDs as global, reading packed flags in the wrong bit order, or sorting by filename. It will silently lose or fabricate rows only when a page begins with a nonzero bit offset, a duplicate has a different ingest position, a signed delta crosses zero, or a new schema reuses a dictionary index. Another common partial solution filters bad pages in the sample query but not in the count and p99 CTEs, producing internally inconsistent reports. A counter-rate implementation that clamps negative rates to zero also looks correct on the sample but fails hidden reset sequences.
tests: Run the entry point on the supplied clean archive and compare the complete report schema, row keys, recovery counts, and metric values with the reference.
Generate hidden archives with reordered files and duplicate pages; check byte-for-byte deterministic report ordering and that each logical measurement is counted once.
Generate hidden archives containing truncation, CRC errors, impossible lengths, and corruption between valid pages; check zero invalid measurements and recovery of later valid pages.

Generate archives using every documented schema version, nontrivial page-local dictionaries, signed deltas spanning negative and positive values, and flag streams whose first record is not byte-aligned.
Compare the recovered measurement relation against the independent reference decoder, requiring at least 99.7% recall and zero false positives.
Compare per-device/day counts, means, anomaly counts, and reset-aware rates against the reference relation.
Compare p99 latency values with a 0.25% relative tolerance, including groups with ties, small counts, and values on both sides of the quantile interpolation boundary.
Check that page-validity, recovered-sample, and report counts remain consistent under injected duplicate and corrupt pages.
Run a large hidden archive with thousands of pages and enforce completion within 12 seconds and bounded memory appropriate for the 2 GB container.

verifier_knob.name: minimum_valid_measurement_recovery
verifier_knob.effect: Raising the threshold makes partial decoders that skip uncommon valid page layouts fail; lowering it allows more corruption-handling and edge-case omissions to pass. The zero-false-positive, p99-tolerance, consistency, and runtime checks remain active.

expected_failure_modes: The solver implements only the visible schema version or assumes one dictionary and flag layout for the whole archive.
The solver uses filename or ingest order as the logical ordering, so duplicate and reordered pages change the result.
The solver gets zigzag sign extension or least-significant-bit packing wrong in rare negative or boundary values.
The solver validates CRC after partially decoding a page and accidentally emits rows from truncated payloads.
The solver repairs the sample relation but leaves validity, recovery metrics, or report aggregates on a different filtering and deduplication path.
The solver calculates counter decreases as zero-rate intervals or huge positive rates instead of excluding the reset-crossing interval.
The solver expands blobs repeatedly through correlated recursive subqueries and meets correctness on the sample but misses the hidden runtime threshold.
The solver verifies only the supplied archive and does not generate cases that expose page-local dictionaries, duplicate identities, bit alignment, or schema transitions.

speedrun: Find the workspace files, documented entry point, and test commands.
Read the README, format documentation, schema declarations, and report contract.
Inspect the entry SQL and all included SQL relations.
Inspect the staging schema and supplied archive fixtures.
Read the archive generator and independent reference decoder.
Read verifier tests and operational/debug logs.
Run the starter pipeline on the clean archive and capture failures.
Query staged pages and generator debug metadata to map headers, trailers, and offsets.
Patch page-bounded validation for lengths, truncation, CRCs, and malformed records.
Patch version dispatch, page-local dictionaries, zigzag deltas, and least-significant-bit-first flags.
Patch logical page identity, duplicate elimination, and order-independent reconstruction.
Materialize one validity relation and make samples, counts, and metrics use the same page key.
Patch reset-aware rates, daily aggregates, anomaly counts, recovery statistics, and p99 calculation.
Run the clean-archive comparison and fix schema, ordering, and numerical mismatches.
Generate targeted archives for reordering, duplicates, corruption, schema transitions, flags, and counter resets.
Run the full visible test suite and compare recovered rows with the reference decoder.
Use EXPLAIN and a large generated archive to find repeated blob expansion or recursive work.
Optimize the decoder and rerun the runtime and memory checks.
Run the final full verifier-equivalent command and inspect the produced report.
invalid_failure_risks: The p99 quantile interpolation method and rounding rules are not stated explicitly; different DuckDB quantile functions could disagree at the tested boundaries.
A relative-error check is undefined when the reference p99 is zero or very close to zero.
The 99.7% recovery threshold needs an explicit rounding rule for archives with few valid measurements.
A hard 12-second limit may be flaky across verifier hosts unless CPU allocation, DuckDB settings, and timing methodology are fixed.
The documented entry point and complete report schema are referenced but not described in the blueprint, so a missing or underspecified fixture contract could make an otherwise correct solution fail.
Deterministic byte-for-byte ordering requires the tie-break order for identical logical records to be documented.
review.reasons: The task is clear, realistic, and mostly verifiable, but the likely solution path is short once the supplied source, generator, and tests are inspected: the principal defects and required repairs are directly discoverable. A strong agent could plausibly complete it in about twenty commands, so genuine difficulty is only 2 under the stated review rule; consequently the scores do not meet the acceptance threshold.
fixes: Specify the exact p99 algorithm, interpolation behavior, numeric precision, zero-reference handling, and report ordering.
Define threshold rounding for 99.7% recovery and the tie-break order for duplicate or otherwise identical records.
Make the verifier use a controlled CPU/memory environment and report separate decoding and end-to-end timing budgets.

To increase genuine difficulty without adding ambiguity, ensure the visible fixture does not expose all failure causes and add hidden interactions combining corruption, schema transitions, duplicate identities, and non-byte-aligned flag streams.
Document the exact entry-point invocation and complete report schema in the task contract rather than relying on workspace discovery.

verdicts.reason: This task concerns recovering and decoding corrupted packed sensor-log pages and computing DuckDB metrics, not authenticated settlement reconciliation of financial spool frames.
This task does not involve release configuration, manifest parsing, Git recovery, SQL translation, or report-audit artifact generation.

Although both involve sensor aggregation and performance constraints, this task centers on decoding and validating damaged versioned archives with recovery semantics rather than correcting fixed-point statistics in a Rust batch aggregator.
This task recovers measurements from packed sensor archives, whereas the reference replays committed transactional event files into canonical JSON snapshots.
This task is an offline SQL-based archive decoder and metrics pipeline, not a persistent replay service reconstructing and mutating catalog state through a JSON protocol.
